Problem

Problem

Retailers picked the minimum, and sellers rejected it

Right after tapping ADD, retailers chose a quantity here. Buying more felt like homework.

  1. 1

    Slab pricing was easy to miss

    Bulk prices, the reason this screen exists, sat in one thin row of small text.

  2. 2

    Policies took the most space

    Payment, delivery and return terms sat above the deals.

  3. 3

    The keypad covered half the screen

    Little room left to compare slabs or show savings.

Why it mattered

The data pointed at one screen

  1. FunnelLowest conversionIn the whole order journey
  2. FeedbackSame screen, every timeThe one right after tapping ADD
  3. Exit rate#1 drop-off pointMore exits than any other step
1–9 pcs

Most orders started this small, and sellers rejected many of them.

Iterations

Three versions, each fixing the last

Could be better

  • Too much info, high cognitive load
  • CTAs too tight for easy tapping
  • No motivation to buy in bulk

Worked well

  • Policies kept per slab
  • Product and qty-price info grouped
  • All slabs upfront, in a familiar vertical list

Could be better

  • Qty and amount kept apart
  • Slab policies removed
  • Still no real push to buy more

Worked well

  • Offers plus a purchase-qty progress bar
  • Lower cognitive load than V1

Trade-offs

  • Policies need other entry points
  • Slabs scroll sideways, so the slab auto-selects as qty changes

Worked well

  • Offers and qty progress motivate
  • Lowest cognitive load of the three
  • Consistent with the app’s design language
  • Intuitive interactions and sound

Before and after

The same screen, redesigned

Before

  • Slabs had little hierarchy and small fonts
  • Primary focus on seller policies
  • Keypad squeezed out slab info

After

  • Margin bar shows which slab you’re in
  • Bigger slab cards with direct actions
  • Shorter keypad with slab-add suggestions

Decisions

Key decisions

Every choice had a reason, and a cost

Aligned with the PM lead, APM and devs at kick-off, wireframes and hi-fi.

  • Policies leave the modal

    They distracted retailers. The cart and seller catalogue now carry them.

  • Show the next win

    Not every slab at once. Slab and savings move with the quantity.

  • Fun as a feature

    Sound and interactions reward moving up a slab.

  • Trade-offs accepted

    Policies live elsewhere, slabs scroll sideways. Both reviewed with dev.

Design journey

How each round tightened one decision

  1. Kick-off

    Agree what this screen is for

    Policies distracted retailers. So the modal does one job: choose a quantity. Policies move to the cart and catalogue. Four goals set.

    Progressive disclosureTrade-offPolicies need other entry points
  2. V1

    Show every slab upfront

    Every slab in a familiar vertical list, so deals compare at a glance.

    Recognition over recallJakob’s lawTrade-offToo much info, high cognitive load
  3. V2

    Add motivation, cut the clutter

    A purchase-qty progress bar and offers make the next slab feel close. Per-slab policies removed.

    Goal-gradient effectHick’s lawTrade-offQty and amount ended up apart
  4. V3 · Final

    Tie quantity, savings and keypad together

    Margin bar and slab cards move live as you type. Qty and total sit together. A shorter keypad adds one-tap slab jumps, plus sound and a gentle MOQ toast.

    Visibility of system statusLaw of proximityFitts’s lawPeak–end ruleTrade-offSlabs scroll sideways
  5. Launch

    Did it work?

    +20% order value and −12% rejected orders, tracked 2 months before vs after.

    +20%order value−12%rejected orders

Stakeholders

Where we disagreed, and how we landed

1

Taking policies out of the modal

Evidence
→
BL

Business / PM lead Their argument

Policies should stay. Seller terms matter, and retailers might miss them elsewhere.

P

Me My counter

Retailers froze on the policies and never used the slabs. This modal’s job is to show every slab and motivate buying more.

How we landed

Policies moved to the cart and seller catalogue, with room to read them. Leads agreed.

In one lineLeads worried about missed seller terms. I showed policies were what people froze on.

2

Vertical list or sideways slabs?

Evidence
→
DV

Dev / APM Their argument

Keep V1’s familiar vertical list. Horizontal scroll is more work and can hide slabs.

P

Me My counter

A vertical list meant scrolling every slab at once: more load, slower choices. Sideways cards reveal offers gradually.

How we landed

V3 shipped with sideways slab cards that auto-select as quantity changes.

In one lineScrolling every slab at once overwhelmed retailers, so slabs went sideways.

3

Use the phone’s default keyboard?

Evidence
→
DV

Dev Their argument

Use the default keyboard. A custom keypad costs more to build and test.

P

Me My counter

The keypad is where slab-add suggestions live, and it’s shorter, so slabs stay visible.

How we landed

V3 kept a shorter custom keypad with slab-add suggestions built in.

In one lineThe custom keypad earns its cost: it carries the slab-add nudges.

Learnings

Reflection

Key takeaways

  1. 🤖

    AI as a thinking partner

    To explore ideas, validate directions and iterate faster. It led to the progress indicator.

  2. 🤝

    Stakeholder alignment sharpens priority

    Agreeing on what mattered put focus on the key decision-making elements.

  3. 👥

    Close cross-functional collaboration

    Continuous feedback helped refine and ship the final design.
